lesson.title: Why Steam Burns Worse: Heat of Vaporization
lesson.summary: The heat of vaporization is the energy needed to convert a liquid to a gas at its boiling point, and for water it is roughly seven times larger than the heat of fusion, which is exactly why steam burns are so much more dangerous than hot water burns.
lesson.body:
The heat of vaporization is the energy required to convert one gram, or one mole, of a substance from liquid to gas at its boiling point, with no change in temperature, exactly the flat boiling plateau on a heating curve. For water, the heat of vaporization is about 2,260 J/g, equivalently about 40.7 kJ/mol, since 40,700 J divided by water's molar mass of 18.02 g/mol gives about 2,259 J/g, consistent within rounding.

Notice that the heat of vaporization for water, 2,260 J/g, is nearly seven times larger than the heat of fusion, 334 J/g: 2,260 divided by 334 works out to about 6.77. This makes physical sense once you think about what each process actually requires. Melting only has to loosen a solid's rigid lattice enough that molecules can slide past each other while remaining close together; most of the intermolecular attraction stays intact in the liquid. Vaporization, by contrast, has to pull molecules essentially all the way apart, from being in constant contact with neighbors in the liquid to being isolated and independent in the gas phase, overcoming nearly all of the intermolecular attraction rather than just loosening it. Fully separating molecules simply takes much more energy than rearranging them.

That large gap has a genuinely dangerous real world consequence: steam burns are much worse than hot water burns at the same temperature. When steam at 100.0 C touches skin, it first has to condense, releasing its full heat of vaporization, before it can cool any further as liquid water. Boiling water at 100.0 C, by contrast, has no such latent heat to release; it can only cool by ordinary sensible heat loss.

Compare the total heat released by 1.00 g of steam at 100.0 C condensing and then cooling to 60.0 C, against 1.00 g of liquid water at 100.0 C simply cooling to 60.0 C, the same final temperature. For the steam: first it condenses, releasing q(condense) = m times the heat of vaporization = (1.00 g)(2,260 J/g) = 2,260 J. Then the resulting liquid water cools from 100.0 C to 60.0 C, releasing q(cool) = mcDeltaT = (1.00 g)(4.184 J/g C)(40.0 C) = 167.4 J. Total heat released by the steam: 2,260 J plus 167.4 J equals 2,427.4 J. For the boiling water with no condensation step, only q(cool) = 167.4 J is released over that same temperature drop. Dividing, 2,427.4 J by 167.4 J is about 14.5, meaning the steam delivers roughly fourteen and a half times more energy to your skin than the same mass of hot water cooling through the same temperature range. That enormous difference, driven entirely by the latent heat of vaporization, is exactly why steam burns cause far deeper tissue damage than a splash of boiling water.
